# Fine-tuning the NLI Model with IPBES-Derived Training Data

## Overview

**Status note (updated):** written while `MoritzLaurer/deberta-v3-large-zeroshot-v2.0`
was the active zero-shot model; it has since been retired in favour of
`MoritzLaurer/bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c` (see `TD_BM_NLI_approach.qmd`'s
"Status update" and the `nli:` comment in `input/config.yaml`). The
fine-tuning procedure below has been retargeted to that model name, but the
exact HuggingFace fine-tuning API for `bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c`'s specific
base architecture has **not** been verified against its model card — check
that before running the script in [Fine-tuning Procedure](#fine-tuning-procedure).

**More importantly, the Training Data Strategy below has been substantially
revised** from the original design. The original recipe treated every paper
cited under a BM as a free, clean `SUPPORTS` example (premise = its
title+abstract, hypothesis = the BM text). Real data now contradicts that
assumption directly: once Phase 2 (LLM verification,
`TD_NLI_LLM_two_phase.qmd`) was extended to review **every** key/seed paper
against its own BM's claim — not just the routed citing-works subset — and
required a verbatim quote before confirming `SUPPORTS`, only **2.6%** of
GA1's 4,783 key-paper pairs actually had explicit textual support in the
title+abstract alone; the rest came back `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO`. A key paper
genuinely *is* the evidence a BM was written from (per IPBES expert
consensus and its own full text), but its **abstract** very often doesn't
restate the specific claim explicitly enough to count as textual entailment
evidence. Training on "abstract text → SUPPORTS" for the ~97% of pairs
where the abstract doesn't actually say that would teach the model to
reproduce topic-adjacency-as-entailment confusion — a real, independently
confirmed failure mode of the current zero-shot model (see
`TD_NLI_LLM_two_phase.qmd`'s discussion of the same GA1 corpus: NLI's own
`SUPPORTS` calls agree with the LLM's grounded, quote-checked verdict only
7% of the time, across NLI's *entire* confidence range, not just at the
margins).

**Revised key insight**: training data is still embedded in the existing
pipeline almost for free, but the *reliable* source is Phase 2's
LLM-verified output (`llm_verification_keypaper_parquet` and
`llm_verification_parquet`), not a blind citation join. Phase 2 already
enforces the one property fine-tuning data needs most — a real, verbatim,
quotable textual anchor for every positive label — so its output can be
used directly with no additional labeling effort, exactly as
`TD_NLI_LLM_two_phase.qmd`'s own "Using LLM Output as Training Data"
section already anticipated for the citing-works chain; the key-paper chain
now extends that same idea to a cleaner, high-precision source.

---

## Training Data Strategy

### Positive examples — LLM-verified SUPPORTS (small, high-precision)

**Not** every paper cited under a BM, unconditionally — see the Status
note above for why that's now known to be unreliable as a training
signal. Instead, use only the key papers Phase 2's full-coverage chain
(`llm_verification_keypaper_parquet`, `R/build_llm_verification_keypaper_parquet.R`)
actually confirmed as `SUPPORTS` with a real, verbatim quote from the
abstract. This is a strict subset of "papers IPBES cites as evidence," but
every example is genuinely grounded in text the premise actually contains,
not just citation provenance — exactly the property fine-tuning data needs.

```r
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

# llm_label == "SUPPORTS" here always has sufficient_evidence == TRUE and a
# verbatim quote (quote_is_verbatim() demotes anything else to
# NOT_ENOUGH_INFO before this table is ever written) -- see
# R/build_llm_verification_parquet.R.
positives <- open_dataset("output/llm_verification/scores_keypaper") |>
  filter(llm_label == "SUPPORTS") |>
  select(assessment, km, bm, claim, work_id, quote) |>
  collect()

# premise here is the QUOTE itself, not the full abstract -- it's the
# minimal text actually shown to have entailed the claim. Re-join the full
# title+abstract from works_parquet instead if you'd rather fine-tune on
# the full premise the pipeline actually scores at inference time (closer
# to the real task, but reintroduces some of the "supporting sentence
# buried in an otherwise off-topic abstract" noise the quote avoids --
# worth comparing both empirically rather than assuming one is better).
positives$hypothesis <- positives$claim
positives$label <- "SUPPORTS"
```

Expected yield: **small** — ~124 for GA1 alone (2.6% of 4,783 key-paper
pairs), growing as more assessments are loaded (IAS is currently disabled
in `input/config.yaml`; re-enabling it and running its own
`llm_verification_keypaper_parquet` would add its share). See
[How Many Examples Are Needed](#how-many-examples-are-needed) below for
what this means for the fine-tuning target.

### Hard negatives — real NLI/LLM disagreements (preferred over synthetic)

The strongest negative source is no longer synthetic — it's real. Every
pair where NLI confidently called `SUPPORTS` (or `REFUTES`) but the
LLM's grounded, quote-checked review said `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO` is a genuine,
in-domain example of the exact failure this fine-tuning effort exists to
correct: topical or citation-provenance adjacency mistaken for entailment.
These come from *both* Phase 2 chains — the main citing-works corpus
(`output/llm_verification/scores`) and the key-paper chain
(`output/llm_verification/scores_keypaper`) — and, unlike the synthetic
cross-BM construction below, need no manual spot-checking of label
correctness, since the LLM's own verbatim-quote requirement already did
that verification.

```r
real_negatives <- function(path) {
  open_dataset(path) |>
    filter(nli_label %in% c("SUPPORTS", "REFUTES"), !uncertain, llm_label == "NOT_ENOUGH_INFO") |>
    select(assessment, km, bm, claim, work_id, nli_label, nli_confidence) |>
    collect()
}
negatives <- bind_rows(
  real_negatives("output/llm_verification/scores"),
  real_negatives("output/llm_verification/scores_keypaper")
)
negatives$hypothesis <- negatives$claim
negatives$label <- "NOT_ENOUGH_INFO"
```

Expected yield: large relative to the positives above — for GA1's citing-works
chain alone this is ~177,000 rows (the same 93% of NLI's confident calls
the LLM downgraded; see `TD_NLI_LLM_two_phase.qmd`'s discussion of this
corpus). Downsample to roughly match the positive count for class balance
(see below) rather than using all of it — a 93%-negative training set would
just teach the model to always predict `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO`.

**Fallback, if more negative volume is needed than the real-disagreement
source provides** (unlikely, given the yield above, but kept as a documented
option): the original synthetic cross-BM pairing still works as a
supplementary source. Same caution as before — prefer cross-KM or
cross-assessment pairs, and spot-check ~20 manually, since topically
adjacent BMs within the same KM may genuinely overlap.

```r
# Supplementary only -- see caution above
set.seed(42)
works <- open_dataset("output/works") |>
  select(assessment, km, bm, title, abstract) |>
  collect()
bms <- open_dataset("output/key_messages") |>
  select(assessment, km, bm, bm_description) |>
  collect()
cited <- works |> inner_join(bms, by = c("assessment", "km", "bm")) |>
  filter(!is.na(abstract), nchar(abstract) > 50) |>
  transmute(premise = paste(title, abstract, sep = ". "), hypothesis = bm_description)
synthetic_negatives <- cited |>
  group_by(hypothesis) |>
  slice_sample(n = 5) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    hypothesis = sample(unique(cited$hypothesis), n(), replace = TRUE),
    label      = "NOT_ENOUGH_INFO"
  ) |>
  filter(paste(premise, hypothesis) %in% paste(cited$premise, cited$hypothesis) == FALSE)
```

### REFUTES examples — the hard class

`REFUTES` is genuinely rare in this domain: papers do not typically directly contradict
IPBES consensus statements. A small real, LLM-quote-verified source now exists too —
`nli_label == "REFUTES" & llm_label == "REFUTES"` in the same `output/llm_verification/scores*`
tables the positives/negatives above come from (105 rows for GA1's citing-works chain;
smaller still for key papers, since key papers should essentially never genuinely
contradict their own BM) — but it's too small on its own for a full class. Options,
in increasing effort, to supplement it:

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| Use the real `REFUTES`/`REFUTES` rows only | Cleanest signal available, but likely too few (~100s) for a full class on its own |
| Omit `REFUTES` entirely | Collapse into `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO`; simplest, acceptable if downstream use only cares about SUPPORTS vs. not |
| Synthetic negation | Negate the BM hypothesis text ("Biodiversity is *not* declining…") and use known-support premises — artificial but gives the model the class signal; combine with the real rows above rather than replacing them |
| Manual labeling | Ask a domain expert to identify a small set (~20–30) of papers that genuinely contradict a BM; gold standard but expensive |

For a first fine-tuning pass, the recommended approach is to **use the real
`REFUTES`/`REFUTES` rows as-is and otherwise omit or use synthetic
negation** to round out the class, then revisit once you have validated
model performance on SUPPORTS vs. NOT_ENOUGH_INFO.

---

## How Many Examples Are Needed?

Fine-tuning a pre-trained NLI model is not training from scratch — the model already
understands the NLI task. You are teaching it to apply that understanding to a new
domain. This requires far fewer examples than original training.

| Examples per class | Expected outcome |
|---|---|
| < 100 | Marginal improvement; high variance across runs |
| 100–300 | Noticeable domain adaptation; worth doing |
| 300–1000 | Solid fine-tuning; diminishing returns above ~500 for a single domain |
| > 1000 | Strong adaptation; useful if you have multiple assessments |

**Practical target:** aim for **300–500 SUPPORTS** and an equal number of
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO negatives (balanced classes). With the revised LLM-verified
positive source, GA1 alone (~124) falls short of even the 100-300 band —
this is the real tradeoff of switching from "free but noisy" to "small but
correct." Options, not mutually exclusive:

- **Combine assessments** before fine-tuning (re-enable IAS in
  `input/config.yaml`, run its own `llm_verification_keypaper_parquet`, and
  pool both) — the doc's own recommendation elsewhere
  ([Single Combined Model vs. Assessment-Specific Models](#single-combined-model-vs-assessment-specific-models))
  to train on all assessments together applies here too.
- **Accept a smaller fine-tuning run** (< 100 examples per class) and
  expect a marginal, high-variance result per the table above — still
  worth trying as a first pass, since the alternative (the original
  recipe's few-thousand noisy positives) risks teaching the model the
  wrong thing rather than nothing.
- **Augment cautiously** with the raw key-paper join (the original
  recipe), but as a clearly lower-confidence, separately-weighted tier
  rather than mixed in as equally-trustworthy `SUPPORTS` labels — e.g. a
  `source` column (`llm_verified` vs. `citation_only`) carried through to
  fine-tuning so the two tiers can be compared or weighted differently
  rather than silently blended.

Hold out 15–20% as a validation set before training.

---

## Do You Need Negatives?

Yes. The model needs to see both classes during fine-tuning or it will over-predict
`SUPPORTS`. The real NLI/LLM disagreement source above already gives far more
negatives than positives — downsample it to roughly match the positive count
for class balance (see above) rather than needing the synthetic cross-BM
construction to manufacture negatives from nothing, as the original design
assumed. Spot-check a sample of whichever source you end up using (~20
pairs) before training regardless, same as the original recommendation.

---

## Fine-tuning Procedure

### Environment

```bash
pip install transformers datasets torch accelerate scikit-learn
```

### Script outline (Python)

```python
from datasets import Dataset
from transformers import (
    AutoTokenizer,
    AutoModelForSequenceClassification,
    TrainingArguments,
    Trainer,
)
import pandas as pd
import torch

# Retargeted to the currently active model (see Status note above) --
# NOT verified against bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c's own model card yet. This
# base model may not load cleanly via a generic
# AutoModelForSequenceClassification(ignore_mismatched_sizes=True) the way
# deberta-v3-large-zeroshot-v2.0 did -- check the model card's own
# fine-tuning guidance (or its base architecture, bge-m3) before assuming
# this script runs unmodified.
MODEL_ID = "MoritzLaurer/bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c"
LABEL2ID  = {"SUPPORTS": 0, "REFUTES": 1, "NOT_ENOUGH_INFO": 2}
ID2LABEL  = {v: k for k, v in LABEL2ID.items()}

# --- Load data (export positives/negatives from R as CSV first) ---
df = pd.read_csv("training_pairs.csv")   # columns: premise, hypothesis, label
df["label_id"] = df["label"].map(LABEL2ID)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)

def tokenize(batch):
    return tokenizer(
        batch["premise"],
        batch["hypothesis"],
        truncation=True,
        max_length=512,
        padding="max_length",
    )

dataset = Dataset.from_pandas(df[["premise", "hypothesis", "label_id"]])
dataset = dataset.rename_column("label_id", "labels")
dataset = dataset.map(tokenize, batched=True)
dataset = dataset.train_test_split(test_size=0.15, seed=42)

model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    num_labels=3,
    id2label=ID2LABEL,
    label2id=LABEL2ID,
    ignore_mismatched_sizes=True,   # classifier head is re-initialised
)

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir        = "nli-ipbes-finetuned",
    num_train_epochs  = 3,
    per_device_train_batch_size = 16,
    per_device_eval_batch_size  = 32,
    evaluation_strategy = "epoch",
    save_strategy       = "epoch",
    load_best_model_at_end = True,
    metric_for_best_model  = "eval_loss",
    fp16 = torch.cuda.is_available(),
    logging_steps = 20,
)

trainer = Trainer(
    model         = model,
    args          = args,
    train_dataset = dataset["train"],
    eval_dataset  = dataset["test"],
)

trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("nli-ipbes-finetuned/best")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("nli-ipbes-finetuned/best")
```

### Compute

A single fine-tuning run on ~600 examples takes roughly **10–20 minutes** on a RunPod
L4 GPU — the same instance already used for inference. No additional infrastructure
needed.

---

## Evaluation

`train_nli.py` prints a `classification_report` on the held-out fold and writes
it to `run_results.json`, but **that is a monitoring aid, not the evaluation**:
it covers one model, on a fold that exists only inside that run. The real
evaluation — every model including the untuned baseline, on one fixed fold — is
the benchmark described in the next section.

Also **manually inspect** 20-30 predictions on citing papers from
`works_citing_parquet` (papers the model has never seen) before running a full
pipeline rebuild. No aggregate number substitutes for reading a few.

## Benchmarking: held-out evaluation across every model

**Status: implemented 2026-09-28.** The `split` column, `train_nli.py`'s use of
it, the local scorer and the four benchmark targets are all live. Every figure quoted below was
measured on that date against the live `output/nli_training/`,
`output/llm_verification/scores*` and `output/nli_scores_evidence*` trees; the
corpus grows continuously, so treat them as a snapshot that establishes *orders
of magnitude and ratios*, not as values to be re-quoted later without
re-measuring.

What follows is the design and, more importantly, the reasoning — particularly about what this
benchmark can and cannot establish, which turned out to be the most important
part.

### Why the numbers we have cannot answer the question

Two fine-tuned checkpoints exist
(`output/nli_training_finetuned/KP=GA1_IAS/citing=GA1/downsample_seed=13/date=2026.09.01_11_30/`
and `.../date=2026.09.01_13_20/`), each with a `run_results.json` carrying a
classification report. Those reports cannot be used to decide whether
fine-tuning helped, for three independent reasons.

#### The evaluation split leaks

`scripts/training/train_nli.py` currently calls

```python
dataset = dataset.train_test_split(test_size=0.15, seed=42)
```

which splits **by row**. The training set is 2,436 rows over only **465
distinct claims** — a mean of 5.2 citing works per claim, up to 72 for the
largest. A random row split therefore places some of nearly every claim's works
in the training fold and the rest in the evaluation fold, with the *identical
hypothesis string* on both sides.

This matters more than the usual hand-wringing about leakage, because the
label is not uniformly distributed over claims: the 562 REFUTES rows are
concentrated in 191 claims. "Recognise this particular claim, predict REFUTES"
is an available shortcut that scores well on the evaluation fold and transfers
to nothing. We do not know how much of the reported performance it accounts
for, and that is precisely the problem.

#### The runs are not comparable to each other

The split is computed inside the training run, from whatever data that run
loaded, after downsampling. Two runs over different data — or the same data
with a different `--downsample-seed` — evaluate on different rows. There is no
fixed yardstick, so run-to-run differences confound "better model" with
"easier evaluation fold".

#### The baseline was never measured

Nothing has ever scored the zero-shot model
(`MoritzLaurer/bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c`) on the evaluation fold. A fine-tuned
model's F1 in isolation says nothing about whether fine-tuning was worth doing;
the comparison that matters was never run.

### The shape of the labelled pool

Anything built here has to respect the structure of the data, which is
lumpier than a row count suggests.

| | |
|---|---:|
| rows | 2,436 |
| distinct claims (`hypothesis`) | 465 |
| distinct Background Messages (`assessment`, `km`, `bm`) | 141 |
| distinct citing/seed works (`work_id`) | 690 |

| class | rows |
|---|---:|
| SUPPORTS | 937 |
| NOT_ENOUGH_INFO | 937 |
| REFUTES | 562 |

Works per claim: median 3, mean 5.2, max 72. Claims per work: median 1, mean
3.5, max 99. **Both axes repeat**, which is why neither a row split nor a
naive split on one key is sufficient.

REFUTES — the class the whole project exists to find — is spread over 191
claims in 56 Background Messages, and is heavily concentrated by assessment:

| assessment | SUPPORTS | NOT_ENOUGH_INFO | REFUTES |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GA1 | 123 | 123 | 421 |
| IAS | 749 | 749 | 137 |
| TCA | 24 | 24 | 2 |
| VA | 41 | 41 | 2 |

558 of 562 REFUTES come from GA1 and IAS. Whether anything learned here
generalises to an assessment outside that pair is an open question the
benchmark should *report on* rather than quietly average away.

### What the benchmark measures, and against what

**It measures agreement with `gpt-4o-mini`.** Every label in
`output/nli_training/` originates in Phase 2's grounded, quote-checked LLM
verdict. Fine-tuning distils that judgment into the NLI model; benchmarking
scores how well the distillation worked. It does not measure truth, and no
amount of held-out discipline turns it into a measurement of truth. The LLM's
verdicts have never been checked against human labels.

This is a ceiling, not a flaw — distilling an expensive accurate judge into a
cheap one is the point of the exercise. But it must be stated wherever the
numbers are, because "94% accurate" invites a reading the data does not
support. See *Two gaps this design does not close* below.

### The split

#### Grouped by Background Message

The grouping key is `(assessment, bm)` — 99 groups — and it deliberately
**omits `km`**. That omission is the least obvious decision here, and it was
found by the verification rather than by reasoning.

A Background Message belongs to several Key Messages. The same `bm` therefore
appears under several `km` values carrying byte-identical claim text: VA's `C9`
sits under `KM7`, `KM8` and `KM9`. Keying on `(assessment, km, bm)` splits one
Background Message into several groups, which the hash then scatters across
both folds. Measured directly:

| grouping key | groups | claim strings in **both** folds |
|---|---:|---:|
| `assessment` + `km` + `bm` | 141 | **126** |
| `assessment` + `bm` | 99 | **0** |

The finer-looking key was the leakier one. The first implementation used it, on
exactly the assumption stated above — that claims never span BMs — and the leak
check caught it immediately. This is what that check is for, and it is why the
benchmark reports `claims_in_both_folds` on every run rather than trusting the
grouping once.

BM-level was chosen over claim-level (465 groups) deliberately. Claims within a
BM are segmented from the same source text and share topic, vocabulary and
often most of their citing works; splitting between them would leak nearly as
much as splitting by row, just less visibly. The cost is fewer groups and
therefore a noisier estimate, which is the right trade: an honest noisy number
beats a precise misleading one.

#### Hash-assigned, not shuffled

```r
hash_bucket <- function(key, salt) {
  vapply(
    paste(key, salt, sep = "|"),
    \(k) strtoi(substr(digest::digest(k, algo = "md5", serialize = FALSE), 1, 6), 16L) %% 100L,
    integer(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE
  )
}
```

`serialize = FALSE` hashes the string bytes directly rather than an R
serialisation of them, so the assignment is stable across R and `digest`
versions — which a benchmark meant to outlive several of both actually needs.

A BM's fold is a pure function of its own identity. Adding an assessment,
re-running Phase 2, or growing the citing-works corpus never moves an existing
BM across the boundary. A shuffled split would silently invalidate every
previously recorded result the moment the corpus grew — and this corpus grows
continuously, which is exactly the condition under which shuffling is worst.

**What is guaranteed, and what is not.** The *fold definition* is stable: which
BMs are test BMs never changes. The *fold contents* are not frozen — reviewing
more pairs under an existing test BM adds rows to the test fold. Observed
directly: clearing GA1's key-paper backlog took the holdout from 467 to 1,205
rows without a single BM changing sides.

The consequence is operational. Because every model is re-scored on the current
fold each time the benchmark runs, a single benchmark run is always internally
comparable — that is the comparison that matters. But numbers from *different*
benchmark runs are not comparable to each other, and a result table should carry
the fold size it was computed against. What hash assignment buys is that a model
trained a year ago can still be scored fairly today; it does not mean a number
printed a year ago is still the right number.

#### Salted, so re-cutting is deliberate

`salt = "bench-v1"` is the version tag. Changing it re-cuts the benchmark; that
is the only way the benchmark should ever change, and the string makes the
change visible in a diff and quotable in a result table.

#### Residual leakage, quantified rather than engineered away

A work can be cited under several Background Messages (up to 99 claims, mean
3.5), so a minority of abstracts will appear in both folds, paired with
different claims. This is a genuine but much weaker leak than claim-text
leakage: the model sees the premise before, never the premise-hypothesis pair
or its label.

Closing it properly means a connected-component split on the (claim, work)
bipartite graph, which at 2,436 rows produces few, huge, unbalanced components
— trading a small measurable bias for a large unmeasurable one. The design
instead **reports the cross-fold work overlap as a diagnostic** alongside every
result, so a reader can judge it.

As realised, that overlap is **62 of 683 distinct works (9.1%)** — but those 62
are the heavily-cited ones, so they account for **55.2% of the test fold's
rows**. That is higher than "a minority of abstracts" suggests and should be
read alongside every number in the report. It is not claim-text leakage and it
is not a reason to distrust the comparison *between* models, all of which face
it identically; it is a reason to treat the absolute level of any single
model's performance as optimistic.

#### The resulting folds

| | train | test |
|---|---:|---:|
| rows | 1,969 | 467 |
| groups (assessment + bm) | 82 | 17 |
| SUPPORTS | 802 | 135 |
| NOT_ENOUGH_INFO | 775 | 162 |
| REFUTES | 392 | 170 |

19.2% of rows held out against a 0.2 target — hash assignment balances group
*count*, not row count, and 17 of 99 groups is 17.2%. All four assessments with
data appear in both folds. The headline subset (NLI said SUPPORTS, truth is
REFUTES) has **111 rows** in the test fold, which is what makes the primary
metric measurable at all.

#### Held out before downsampling, never after

`train_nli.py` now takes the holdout out **first** and balances only the train
fold. The order is not cosmetic: `--downsample-seed` caps every class to the
smallest, so downsampling a combined pool and splitting afterwards would make
the evaluation set itself a function of the seed. Two runs with different seeds
would then be scored on different rows — reintroducing, by a different route,
exactly the run-to-run incomparability the fixed holdout exists to remove.

On the current pool that means 1,969 train rows balanced down to 392 per class
(1,176 total), against a 467-row test fold left at its natural, mildly
imbalanced composition. The evaluation fold is deliberately *not* balanced: it
is meant to resemble the data, not the training regime.

### What to report

The default `classification_report` headline is actively misleading here, and
should not be the number anyone quotes.

#### Not accuracy

After `--downsample-seed` caps every class to the smallest, training and
evaluation are near-balanced three-way. Deployment is not: REFUTES is 0.2–3% of
pairs depending on the route. A balanced-set accuracy flatters every model
equally and predicts nothing about behaviour on the real stream.

#### REFUTES precision and recall, separately

Stated as two numbers, never combined into F1 for the headline. The project's
tolerance for the two errors is not symmetric — a missed refutation is a
finding that never surfaces, a false one is a claim a human discards in
seconds — and F1 assumes it is.

#### The SUPPORTS→REFUTES flip rate

This is the number that decides whether fine-tuning worked.

Tracing every confirmed refutation back to what the zero-shot NLI had said
about that same pair:

| NLI said | citing works | key papers | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| SUPPORTS | 303 | 34 | **337 (60%)** |
| REFUTES | 105 | 76 | 181 (32%) |
| NOT_ENOUGH_INFO | 0 | 44 | 44 (8%) |

Only 32% of confirmed refutations were pairs the zero-shot model flagged
REFUTES. The **largest single source, 60%, is pairs it confidently called
SUPPORTS** and the LLM overturned. The zero-shot model did not merely miss
those — it got them backwards.

So the benchmark's primary metric is: *of the evaluation-fold rows where NLI
said SUPPORTS and the LLM said REFUTES, what fraction does each model now call
REFUTES?* If a fine-tuned checkpoint does not move that number, it has not done
the job this project needs, whatever its macro-F1 says.

(The zero in the citing-works `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO` row is an artefact of routing,
not a finding — see below.)

#### A threshold sweep, not one operating point

Phase 1 stores the full probability distribution and every threshold decision
is made downstream in `dplyr`. The benchmark should match that: emit
precision/recall across the confidence range per model, not a single argmax
operating point. This also yields the re-calibrated deployment threshold, which
a balanced evaluation set's argmax cannot — the base-rate shift between a 1:1:1
training distribution and a 0.2% deployment stream guarantees an argmax
classifier over-predicts REFUTES in production.

#### Per-assessment breakdown

Given 558 of 562 REFUTES come from GA1+IAS, a pooled number mostly measures
those two. Report TCA and VA separately even though their counts are tiny; "we
cannot tell" is a legitimate and useful result.

### Three human-labelled artifacts, none of which exist yet

These are routinely conflated and they measure different things. All three were
discussed and none has been built; this records what each is for, so the next
person does not build one and believe they have another.

Everything in this document so far measures **agreement with `gpt-4o-mini`**.
Its verdicts are the training labels, and the benchmark scores how faithfully a
fine-tuned model reproduces them. A model that perfectly reproduced a wrong
judge would score perfectly. Nothing here breaks that circle — these three do.

#### 1. Gold standard — adjudicate labels that already exist

Humans re-judge a sample of pairs that **already have LLM verdicts**: was
gpt-4o-mini right? Gives the judge's accuracy, which is the ceiling on every
number in this document.

Sample **stratified by label**, not uniformly: REFUTES is ~0.5% of verdicts, so
a uniform draw of 300 contains one or two. Weight toward REFUTES and toward the
cases where NLI and the LLM disagree, which is where the errors were found by
reading. `output/tables/refutes_review.csv` is the first slice of this, already
generated with empty `human_verdict`/`human_note` columns.

**What it cannot do:** it only covers pairs that were *routed* for review, so it
inherits Phase 2's routing bias. It measures the judge, not the pipeline.

#### 2. Curated test set — evaluation that owes nothing to any model

Humans judge `(claim, paper)` pairs drawn **independently of model output** —
ideally a random sample of the corpus, including pairs no model flagged. This is
the only artifact that can say whether the pipeline finds what is actually
there, rather than whether it agrees with itself.

It can serve the benchmark **and** training, but **not both with the same rows**:
training on it and evaluating on it is leakage of exactly the kind the holdout
exists to prevent. Split it by the same `(assessment, bm)` hash the rest of the
benchmark uses, so the curated rows land in train/test consistently with
everything else.

Sizing is governed by REFUTES, as always. At the corpus base rate (0.2-3%
depending on route) a random sample large enough to contain 50 refutations is
thousands of pairs of human reading. Stratifying by NLI output makes it
affordable but reintroduces a model-shaped bias — an honest compromise is a
*two-stratum* design: a small uniform-random stratum that supports unbiased
rate estimates, plus a larger enriched stratum that supplies enough REFUTES to
train or evaluate on, with the inclusion probabilities recorded so the two can
be reweighted.

#### 3. Threshold validation for the relevance screen

Humans judge pairs the Jev screen scores **below** a candidate threshold: was
the screen right that this paper does not bear on the claim?

This is the only one with a hard deadline attached to a decision: at 0.3 the
screen discards ~24% of true SUPPORTS, and a wrongly dropped pair is never
reviewed and leaves no trace — no verdict, no failed quote check, nothing to
audit. `relevance_screen.threshold` stays `~` until this exists.

Sample from the **dropped** side specifically. Validating the kept side measures
nothing useful: those pairs go to the LLM anyway.

#### Practical notes for all three

**Two reviewers on at least a subset.** Inter-annotator agreement is the real
ceiling: if two experts agree 75% on REFUTES, no model can be asked to beat 75%,
and a model at 70% is near-ceiling rather than failing. Without that number the
other two artifacts are uninterpretable.

**Record the reviewer and the date per row**, not just the verdict. Judgements
drift, reviewers disagree, and a disagreement that cannot be attributed cannot be
resolved.

**`label_source` is already a column** in the training set (`source`), carrying
`llm_verified` today. Human rows enter as a different value and
`build_nli_training_data()` can weight or filter on it with no restructuring --
the slot was left open deliberately.

### Two gaps this design does not close

Both should be visible in the rendered report rather than buried here, because
each bounds what the headline number means.

#### The holdout cannot measure recall

It inherits Phase 2's routing bias. For citing works, only `REFUTES-certain`
(9,054 pairs) and `SUPPORTS-certain` (181,705 pairs) were ever sent for LLM
review. Pairs the zero-shot model called `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO` — 1,232,027 in GA1
alone — have never been reviewed, so no genuine refutation hiding among them is
in the labelled pool, in the training set, or in any split of it.

The key-paper chain is full-coverage and gives the only direct estimate:

| what NLI said | pairs reviewed | LLM confirmed REFUTES | rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| REFUTES | 2,457 | 76 | 3.09% |
| NOT_ENOUGH_INFO | 11,905 | 44 | 0.37% |

The REFUTES flag is ~8x enriched — real signal — but the NEI pile is 4.8x
larger, so **37% of every refutation found in the full-coverage chain was
sitting in pairs NLI had called NEI**. For citing works in GA1 the NEI pile is
3.8x the REFUTES pile, so the same effect applies at greater scale.

A held-out split of a biased pool measures performance on the bias. Closing
this needs a **recall probe**: a random sample drawn across the *full* NLI
output including NEI, sent through Phase 2 for labelling. A few thousand pairs
is a rounding error against Phase 2's existing spend, and it is the only thing
that can convert "we found 408 refutations" into "we found 408 of an estimated
N".

#### The labels are one model's opinion

562 REFUTES rows, none human-checked. That is a single afternoon's reading, and
it is the highest value-per-unit-effort check available anywhere in this
pipeline: it bounds the ceiling every other number here is measured against.

The design therefore treats the label source as a **column, not an
assumption** — the benchmark reads `(premise, hypothesis, label, label_source)`
and a human-labelled set with `label_source = "human"` drops into the same
targets with no restructuring. Retrofitting a second label source into a report
built for one is the expensive way to do this; leaving the slot open costs
nothing today.

### Where it lives: the training project, not a fifth one

The benchmark is **four targets inside `_targets_training.R`**, not a project of
its own. A fifth project was designed first and rejected; the reasoning is
worth recording, because "add a project" was the obvious move and it is wrong.

#### The existing split criterion does not extend

The four projects in [TD_targets](TD_targets.html) are divided on cost,
credentials and blast radius — collection has OpenAlex and a destructive
rebuild, fact checking has GPU hours and OpenRouter, training has OpenRouter
and a 25-minute local fine-tune, reporting has none. Benchmarking has none
either, but `reporting` earns its separation by serving **all four** projects,
whereas a benchmark only ever looks at what training produced.

`TD_targets.qmd`'s own test is whether something is a separate process
sharing an input, or a stage of one process. Benchmarking is the evaluation
half of training: nobody runs it without caring about a training run. That is
the second case, and it belongs in the same DAG.

#### The cost ratio

As its own project the benchmark is roughly twelve targets — of which five are
pure diagram overhead (`mmd_workflow_*`, `diagram_*`, `r_files`,
`pipeline_mmd`) and three are re-declared configuration — plus a documentation
tax of nine touchpoints: two CLAUDE.md tables, the README table, the four
`workflow_*.mmd` headers that each enumerate the project set, the Shiny node
metadata, the diagram selector, and TD_targets' Running section. Every one of
those is a place the set can drift out of sync, and several already have.

Inside the training project it is four targets reusing `config_file`,
`nli_active`, `granularity`, `r_files` and the existing diagram chain.

#### The decisive reason: a better dependency edge becomes available

`nli_finetuned_model` is already a `format = "file"` target, so the training
project already hashes its output. Taking it as a **bare, never-read argument**
— the convention this codebase already uses three times (`nli_scores_qa_data` ←
`nli_scores_keypaper_evidence`, `nli_finetuned_model` ← `nli_training_data`,
`llm_verification_parquet` ← `nli_scores_by_claim_evidence`) — makes a new
checkpoint invalidate the benchmark automatically, at no additional cost.

Across a project boundary that edge is not available: the benchmark would have
to re-declare the 42 GB `output/nli_training_finetuned/` tree as its own
tracked input, which `reporting` already refuses to do for exactly this reason.
The separate-project design was therefore forced into scanning the directory
untracked and *documenting a manual re-run step* — a wart that disappears
entirely by folding in.

So the design uses **both** mechanisms, for two different jobs:

- **Enumeration** — scan disk for every checkpoint to benchmark, since runs
  accumulate and no config key tracks them (the same instinct
  `shiny_app/R/discover_artifacts.R` applies to rendered artifacts).
- **Invalidation** — the bare `nli_finetuned_model` argument, so producing a new
  checkpoint marks the benchmark stale without anyone remembering to.

One consequence to know: because `benchmark_scores` now depends on
`nli_finetuned_model`, naming it in a `tar_make()` while that target is
outdated will start a real fine-tuning run. Use `shortcut = TRUE` to benchmark
the checkpoints already on disk — the same discipline every paid target in this
repository already requires.

#### When to split it out after all

Cheaply, and exactly as steps 2 and 3 of the pipeline split did — the targets
move verbatim. Two things would justify it: a second input the training project
does not have (the recall probe over the full NLI output, or a human gold set
with its own labelling workflow), or wanting to benchmark models training never
produced, such as a different base model or an external checkpoint. Either
makes it a genuinely separate process. Until one exists, a fifth project is
structure built for a future that may not arrive.

### Models under test

Discovered from disk, never from configuration:

```r
c(
  benchmark_config$baseline_model,  # MoritzLaurer/bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c
  grep("/best$", list.dirs("output/nli_training_finetuned", recursive = TRUE), value = TRUE)
)
```

Three entries today. Each checkpoint's path is already its identity
(`KP=GA1_IAS/citing=GA1/downsample_seed=13/date=2026.09.01_11_30`), so it
doubles as the output partition key and the result-table row label with no
naming scheme to invent. The `.disabled/<nli_config>/` marker directory written
when `training.finetune.enabled` is false contains no `best/` and is skipped by
the same pattern.

### Serving the models

**Local CPU, not RunPod.** The NLI pool serves one model per deployment, so
comparing three models through it means three deployments — real money, real
setup, and a confound if their hardware differs. The evaluation fold is a few
hundred rows; three models over it is minutes of local CPU using the same
`transformers` stack and the same venv `train_nli.py` already requires.

`scripts/benchmark/score_nli_local.py --model <path|hf-id>` mirrors
`train_nli.py`'s model/tokenizer loading and writes per-row probabilities;
`R/build_nli_benchmark_scores.R` bridges to it exactly as
`R/build_nli_finetuned_model.R` already bridges to `train_nli.py` — a thin
`system2()` wrapper whose output directory is a real `format = "file"` target.

`score_nli_local.py` reproduces `server.py` rather than inventing a scheme,
because a baseline scored differently from how it is deployed is not a
baseline. The mode is derived from the model itself — does its `id2label` carry
all three real label names? — not from a flag, so a model cannot be scored in
the wrong mode by misconfiguration. Verified against real deployed scores: on
clean abstracts the local probabilities reproduce the production server's
`nli_confidence` to about four decimal places.

**One inexactness, recorded because it is real.** The deployed pipeline cleans
the premise (`clean_title()`/`clean_abstract()` strip HTML/JATS/LaTeX) while
`train_nli.py` — and therefore this benchmark — uses the raw `title`/`abstract`
stored in the training set. The comparison *between* models is unaffected, since
all of them see the same premises; but the baseline row is a close rather than
exact reproduction of deployed behaviour, and divergence concentrates in
marked-up abstracts.

`max_length` also differs by mode and is recorded per model in the output: the
zero-shot model is scored at the config's deployed 2048, a fine-tuned
checkpoint at the 512 it was trained on, because running it longer at inference
would be out of distribution. Truncation counts are reported so this is visible
rather than assumed harmless.

Note `train_nli.py` forces `use_cpu=True` because MPS was measured to produce
`grad_norm == 0.0` at this sequence length *and* to be slower. Inference is a
different workload and MPS may well be fine here, but the benchmark's job is
comparability, not speed: pin CPU so results are reproducible, and revisit only
if runtime becomes a real constraint.

### Rendering stays in `reporting`

The benchmark writes `output/tables/nli_benchmark_qa.rds` — the same
cached-rds-holding-a-prebuilt-widget convention every other QA data builder
here uses, because the qmd renders in a fresh session that never sources
`R/*.R`. The reporting project declares that path as a `format = "file"` target
keeping the producer's name, and
`input/reports/QA_NLI_Benchmark_Report.qmd` reads it.

That is the one genuine cross-project edge this design adds, and it runs the
same direction as every other one: everything renders in `reporting`, nothing
else renders anything.

### What this changes upstream

Adding the `split` column to `build_nli_training_data()` invalidates
`nli_training_data` and therefore `nli_finetuned_model`. **Both existing
checkpoints need retraining before their numbers mean anything** — they were
trained on a leaking split, so they have seen evaluation-fold claims. That is
not a cost of the benchmark; it is the benchmark's first finding. Keep the old
run directories rather than overwriting them: "trained with a leaking split" is
a useful comparison row, and the cheapest evidence available for how much the
leak was worth.

### An incidental finding: 90% of the checkpoint tree is dead weight

Measured while checking what the bare `nli_finetuned_model` edge would cost to
hash. One run directory:

| | |
|---|---:|
| `checkpoint-89` | 6.3 GB |
| `checkpoint-178` | 6.3 GB |
| `checkpoint-267` | 6.3 GB |
| `best/` | 2.1 GB |
| `run_results.json` | 8 KB |

19 of every 21 GB is HuggingFace `Trainer`'s intermediate saves, and nothing
reads them: `build_nli_finetuned_model_qa_data.R` reads `run_results.json`, the
benchmark reads `best/`. A checkpoint is 6.3 GB because it carries AdamW
optimiser state (roughly twice the parameters) on top of the 2.1 GB of weights;
`best/` is `save_model()`, weights only.

`save_total_limit=1` is now set in `TrainingArguments`, which keeps one
checkpoint instead of one per epoch — 8.4 GB per run rather than 21 GB.
`load_best_model_at_end` still works: Trainer always retains the best
checkpoint under the limit. Dropping checkpoints entirely after `best/` is
written would reach 2.1 GB, but leaves no resumption point for a run that dies,
and at 25 minutes a run that is not worth much.

The two pre-existing 21 GB runs are untouched; they predate this and are kept
deliberately as the "trained with a leaking split" comparison.

Unrelated to benchmarking, and worth doing regardless.

### Operating notes

Three things a future reader will otherwise rediscover the hard way.

**`benchmark_scores` is downstream of a ~25 minute training run.** The bare
`nli_finetuned_model` argument that keeps the benchmark honest also means naming
`benchmark_scores` while that target is outdated *starts* a fine-tune. Use
`shortcut = TRUE` to benchmark the checkpoints already on disk. This is a new
path to an accidental local run that did not exist before the benchmark.

**The training store churns more.** The benchmark iterates fast — every metric
tweak — while the fine-tune is slow, so `tar_outdated()` on the training project
shows benchmark noise more often than it used to. Noise, not incorrectness.

**The training store has no metadata for three targets.**
`llm_verification_keypaper_parquet`, `nli_training_data` and
`nli_finetuned_model` were last built in the pre-split `_targets/` store; the
training store has only ever run the NLI chain. So
`tar_make(names = "nli_training_data", shortcut = TRUE)` cannot bootstrap — it
refuses to load a dependency it has never recorded — and building it for real
would route ~945,000 uncached pairs through OpenRouter (~$140, see the backlog
note in `TODO.md`).

The first training set carrying the `split` column, and the first fine-tune
trained on it, were therefore produced by calling `build_nli_training_data()`
and `train_nli.py` **directly**, outside `targets`. What is on disk is exactly
what those targets would have written; what is missing is store bookkeeping,
which fills itself the first time the key-paper Phase 2 spend is authorised.
Worth knowing before reading `tar_outdated()` and concluding the work was not
done.

## Deployment

The fine-tuned model is a drop-in replacement for the original. Update the model path
in the Docker container ([external/runpod/docker/nli-runpod/](external/runpod/docker/nli-runpod/)) and redeploy:

```dockerfile
# In external/runpod/docker/nli-runpod/Dockerfile (or equivalent entrypoint)
# Replace:
MODEL_ID = "MoritzLaurer/bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c"
# With:
MODEL_ID = "/app/nli-ipbes-finetuned/best"   # local path inside container
```

Upload the fine-tuned model directory to the RunPod volume or push to a private
HuggingFace Hub repo, then update the path accordingly.

---

## Single Combined Model vs. Assessment-Specific Models

### Train on all assessments (recommended first approach)

- More total examples → better generalisation
- The model learns "IPBES scientific claim language" broadly — all BMs share a common
  style and conventions regardless of topic area
- A combined model handles a *new* assessment better than one trained on a single
  assessment
- When a new assessment is added, no retraining is needed

### Assessment-specific models

- Only worth considering if assessments cover genuinely distinct vocabulary domains
  (e.g. land degradation vs. marine ecosystems) and per-assessment evaluation reveals
  a clear performance gap
- More maintenance overhead: one model per assessment to deploy, version, and update
- Higher risk of overfitting if a single assessment has few BMs or citations

### Practical middle ground

Train once on all assessments combined, but **evaluate per assessment** — compute F1
separately for each assessment's held-out validation set. If one assessment performs
noticeably worse, a targeted top-up fine-tuning pass can be run starting from the
combined model (not from scratch), using only that assessment's data.

| Scenario | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| First fine-tuning run | Combined model across all assessments |
| New assessment added later | Combined model already generalises; no retraining needed |
| One assessment has clearly worse F1 | Top-up fine-tune from combined model on that assessment's data |
| Assessments have very different domain vocabularies | Evaluate first; split only if evidence warrants it |

Add an `assessment` column to `training_pairs.csv` so you can always filter to a
per-assessment subset for evaluation or top-up training without regenerating the data.

---

## Recommended Steps

1. **Extract positives** from `output/llm_verification/scores_keypaper` filtered to
   `llm_label == "SUPPORTS"` (R script above); export as `training_pairs.csv`
2. **Extract negatives** from the real NLI/LLM disagreement rows in
   `output/llm_verification/scores` and `output/llm_verification/scores_keypaper`
   (both chains); downsample to roughly match the positive count. Fall back to the
   synthetic cross-assessment BM pairing only if more volume is needed; spot-check
   20 pairs manually either way
3. **Check class balance** — target roughly 50/50 SUPPORTS / NOT_ENOUGH_INFO; add
   the real `REFUTES`/`REFUTES` rows (plus synthetic negations if still short) for
   that class
4. **Fine-tune** on RunPod L4 using the script above (~15 min) — confirm
   `bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0-c`'s fine-tuning API first (see the script's own caveat)
5. **Evaluate** on held-out set; compare F1 on SUPPORTS against zero-shot baseline
6. **Spot-check** on a sample from `works_citing_parquet`
7. **Redeploy** Docker container with updated model path
8. **Invalidate** `nli_scores_by_claim_evidence` (and/or `nli_scores_keypaper_evidence`)
   and re-run the pipeline
